title: Why AI Companies Are Buying—And Then Destroying—Old Books

body:
in Books, Technology |   	August 28th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

We’ve long joked about delay­ing bed­time in order to read the entire inter­net, but the prospect of actu­al­ly doing so does­n’t sound as appeal­ing as it used to. An ever-grow­ing pro­por­tion of text online, we may sense, has­n’t been writ­ten by humans, but gen­er­at­ed by arti­fi­cial intel­li­gence. One solu­tion is to return to read­ing on paper, and beyond that, spend­ing our time only with books pub­lished before the advent — and thus uncor­rupt­ed by the out­put — of large lan­guage mod­els. Iron­i­cal­ly, that’s what large lan­guage mod­els them­selves have had to do, and in order to ensure them a steady diet of man­made text, their own­ers are resort­ing to con­tro­ver­sial­ly destruc­tive meth­ods.
Sus­pi­cions first arose when book deal­ers noticed a spike in their income due to large orders from mys­te­ri­ous buy­ers for titles they assumed they’d nev­er unload. Books on home oxy­gen treat­ment in Italy, mar­riage lit­i­ga­tion in medieval Eng­land, Texas civ­il pro­ce­dure in the twen­ty-tens, Swedish com­e­dy in the six­ties: these enti­ties bought them all, and for what­ev­er price the sell­er hap­pened to be ask­ing.
404 Media reporter Emanuel Maiberg tracked the path of one such book, which even­tu­al­ly wound up at a Las Vegas scan­ning facil­i­ty run by Ama­zon. Though under­gird­ed by advanced tech­nol­o­gy, the work done there is sim­ple: dig­i­tize as many books as pos­si­ble, then destroy them.


	

“In order to scan them real­ly fast, they cut the spines off the books and fed the pages to the scan­ner,” Maiberg explained to NPR. Many are tech­ni­cal­ly rare, albeit eso­teric obscu­ri­ties like van­i­ty pub­li­ca­tions and old instruc­tion man­u­als rather than first-edi­tion clas­sics. Humans may not val­ue them, but LLMs do: their con­sump­tion fore­stalls “a prob­lem called mod­el col­lapse, where if an AI trains on AI train­ing data, it gets worse.” Ama­zon and Anthrop­ic have both been found to use the book-sac­ri­fic­ing method to har­vest text, but every com­pa­ny with mod­els to train needs a solu­tion. All this makes for “an unusu­al­ly on-the-nose exam­ple of dig­i­tal tech­nol­o­gy devour­ing lit­er­ary cul­ture,” as the Wall Street Jour­nal’s Melis­sa Korn puts it. But when you real­ly have read the entire inter­net, per­haps extreme mea­sures are inevitable.

He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: The Art of Splendor Solis, the Most Glorious Illuminated Alchemical Manuscript of Them All
description:
in Books, History |   	August 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

When it was pub­lished in the Unit­ed States in 1998, Har­ry Pot­ter and the Phi
body:
in Books, History |   	August 27th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

When it was pub­lished in the Unit­ed States in 1998, Har­ry Pot­ter and the Philoso­pher’s Stone was reti­tled Har­ry Pot­ter and the Sor­cer­er’s Stone. The jokes about the Amer­i­can read­ing pub­lic’s appar­ent aller­gy to the very word philoso­pher write them­selves, but the change was also unfor­tu­nate for more sub­stan­tial rea­sons. A “sor­cer­er’s stone” had no cul­tur­al res­o­nance at all, where­as the philoso­pher’s stone had been sought after since, at the very lat­est, the dawn of the fourth cen­tu­ry. Some sources claim that human knowl­edge of it goes all the way back to Adam, who got the word direct­ly from God. In any case, it’s no mys­tery why the philoso­pher’s stone has long cap­tured the col­lec­tive imag­i­na­tion of human­i­ty, giv­en that it’s reput­ed to turn lead into gold.

Among the rumored pos­ses­sors of the philoso­pher’s stone through­out his­to­ry is Salomon Tris­mosin, a six­teenth-cen­tu­ry Renais­sance alchemist who taught the influ­en­tial physi­cian Paracel­sus. He’s also cred­it­ed, at least in leg­ends, with writ­ing Splen­dor Solis, a book once no less desir­able than the next Har­ry Pot­ter vol­ume in that series’ hey­day.
Noth­ing so mun­dane as “a list of instruc­tions for whip­ping up a lit­tle alchem­i­cal soup in the hope of find­ing a nugget of arti­fi­cial gold in the pot at the end,” writes Jörg Völl­nagel at Medievalists.net, it rather “sets forth the phi­los­o­phy of alche­my, a world view accord­ing to which the human being (the alchemist) exists and acts in har­mo­ny with nature, respect­ing divine cre­ation and at the same time inter­ven­ing in the process­es under­ly­ing that cre­ation, all the while sup­port­ing its growth with the help of alche­my.”
As “a — or rather the – prime exam­ple of an illu­mi­nat­ed alchem­i­cal man­u­script,” Splen­dor Solis has drawn the fas­ci­na­tion of even such mod­ern fig­ures as William But­ler Yeats, James Joyce, and Umber­to Eco. It also became an impor­tant work in the sym­bol­ic-cul­tur­al uni­verse of Carl Jung, who, accord­ing to the Asso­ci­a­tion of Jun­gian Ana­lysts, “rec­og­nized the alchem­i­cal motifs and sym­bols as expres­sions of the indi­vid­u­a­tion process, the trans­for­ma­tion and inte­gra­tion of the psy­che. Splen­dor Solis, with its rich sym­bol­ism and pro­found alle­gories, res­onat­ed with Jung’s under­stand­ing of the arche­typ­al imagery and the trans­for­ma­tive nature of the human psy­che, con­tribut­ing to his the­o­ries on ana­lyt­i­cal psy­chol­o­gy.”

None of this is to say that Jung, or many oth­er esteemed intel­lec­tu­als of the past cou­ple of cen­turies, believed that base met­als real­ly could be trans­mut­ed to gold and sil­ver. But they did under­stand that the phe­nom­e­non of alche­my has much to reveal about the irre­solv­able exis­ten­tial nego­ti­a­tion between man and the world he inhab­its. It res­onates so deeply that it’s even worked in chil­dren’s lit­er­a­ture, and to great com­mer­cial suc­cess at that. You can even feel some of it just by gaz­ing upon Splen­dor Solis’ 22 gold-high­light­ed, book-of-hours-style illus­tra­tions at the web site of M. Moleiro, pub­lish­er of one fac­sim­i­le edi­tion. And who knows? If, as in the world of Har­ry Pot­ter, the philoso­pher’s stone also grants immor­tal­i­ty, per­haps Salomon Tris­mosin still walks some­where among us.
You can view pages of Splen­dor Solis on Wikipedia. Enter the image gallery here.

title: Isaac Asimov Explains His Three Laws of Robots: Do No Harm, Follow Orders, Survive, in That Order
description: A num­ber of futur­ists, philoso­phers, and technophiles believe we are approach­ing what they call the “sin­gu­lar­i­ty”: a point in time wh
body:
A num­ber of futur­ists, philoso­phers, and technophiles believe we are approach­ing what they call the “sin­gu­lar­i­ty”: a point in time when smart machines become much smarter, stronger, and faster than their cre­ators, and then become self-con­scious. What­ev­er the chance of this occur­ring, it’s worth­while to pon­der the con­se­quences. But we do already, all the time—in exis­ten­tial­ly bleak sce­nar­ios like Blade Run­ner, the Ter­mi­na­tor series, the reboot­ed Bat­tlestar Galac­ti­ca (and its failed pre­quel Capri­ca).
The prospects are nev­er pleas­ant. Robot­ic engi­neers in these worlds hard­ly seem to both­er teach­ing their machines the kind of moral code that would keep them from turn­ing and destroy­ing us (that is, when they aren’t explic­it­ly designed to do so).
I won­der about this con­cep­tu­al gap—convenient as it may be in nar­ra­tive terms—given that Isaac Asi­mov, one of the fore­fa­thers of robot fic­tion invent­ed just such a moral code. In the video above, he out­lines it (with his odd pro­nun­ci­a­tion of “robot”). The code con­sists of three laws; in his fic­tion these are hard­wired into each robot’s “positron­ic brain,” a fic­tion­al com­put­er that gives robots some­thing of a human-like con­scious­ness.
First Law: A robot may not injure a human being, or, through inac­tion, allow a human being to come to harm.
Sec­ond Law: A robot must obey the orders giv­en it by human beings except where such orders would con­flict with the First Law.
Third Law: A robot must pro­tect its own exis­tence as long as such pro­tec­tion does not con­flict with the First or Sec­ond Law.
Isaac Asi­mov devot­ed a good deal of his writ­ing career to the sub­ject of robots, so it’s safe to say, he’d done quite a bit of think­ing about how they would fit into the worlds he invent­ed. In doing so, Asi­mov had to solve the prob­lem of how robots would inter­act with humans once they had some degree of free will. But are his three laws suf­fi­cient? Many of Asimov’s sto­ries—I, Robot, for example—turn on some fail­ure or con­fu­sion between them. And even for their chase scenes, explo­sions, and melo­dra­ma, the three screen explo­rations of arti­fi­cial life men­tioned above thought­ful­ly exploit philo­soph­i­cal ambi­gu­i­ties and insuf­fi­cien­cies in Asimov’s sim­ple sys­tem.
For one thing, while Asimov’s robots were hunks of met­al, tak­ing only vague­ly humanoid form, the robots of our cur­rent imag­in­ings emerge from an uncan­ny val­ley with real­is­tic skin and hair or even a genet­ic code and cir­cu­la­to­ry sys­tem. They are pos­si­ble sex­u­al part­ners, friends and lovers, co-work­ers and supe­ri­ors. They can deceive us as to their nature (a fourth law by Bul­gar­i­an nov­el­ist Lyuben Dilov states that a robot “must estab­lish its iden­ti­ty as a robot in all cas­es”); they can con­ceive chil­dren or desires their cre­ators nev­er intend­ed. These dif­fer­ences beg impor­tant ques­tions: how eth­i­cal are these laws? How fea­si­ble? When the sin­gu­lar­i­ty occurs, will Skynet become aware of itself and destroy us?
Unlike Asi­mov, we now live in a time where the ques­tions have direct applic­a­bil­i­ty to robots liv­ing among us, out­side the pages of sci-fi. As Japan­ese and South Kore­an roboti­cists have found, the three laws can­not address what they call “open tex­ture risk”— unpre­dictable inter­ac­tions in unstruc­tured envi­ron­ments. Humans rely on nuanced and often pre­con­scious read­ings of com­plex social codes and the fine shades of mean­ing embed­ded in nat­ur­al lan­guage; despite many advances, machines are still catch­ing up. Whether or not they can suc­cess­ful­ly devel­op it is an open ques­tion, mak­ing humanoid robots with arti­fi­cial intel­li­gence an “open tex­ture risk.” But as you can see from the video below, we’re per­haps much clos­er to Blade Run­ner or, of course, arti­fi­cial intel­li­gence than to the clunky, inter­stel­lar min­ing machines in Asi­mov’s fic­tion.


	

Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2012.

title: Lush Foliage Permeates Xanthe Burdett's Delicate Portraiture
description: For Xanthe Burdett, the boundary between humans and nature is thin, malleable, and always in flux. The Devon-born, London-based artist works large
body:
For Xanthe Burdett, the boundary between humans and nature is thin, malleable, and always in flux. The Devon-born, London-based artist works largely in a palette of greens, layering leaves and vines atop faint figurative silhouettes. Invoking mythology and ancient cosmologies, her paintings suggest that people and plants are not only interconnected but also intrinsically one.
Beginning with a sketch, Burdett employs the Renaissance-era cartoon method of transferring her drawings to canvas, which involves layering a substance like charcoal between the preparatory composition and the substrate and tracing the initial linework. After, the artist adds various greenery until she’s reached a lush density.
“They came upon a clearing” (2026), oil on linen, 70 x 100 centimeters
Burdett considers superimposition to be a way of “reimagining the body as a site of ecological and mythic transformation,” she says. “In an age defined by environmental catastrophe—wildfires, biodiversity loss, and climate anxiety—the work functions both as a refuge and as a space for imagining alternative ways of being with the more-than-human world.”
Presented as “host and terrain,” Burdett’s figures encompass a sense of growth and regeneration as “flesh gives way to nettles, brambles, and tender green shoots,” she adds. Many also invoke mythic deities, including Venus, the Roman god of beauty and fertility, and Janus, the god of transitions and beginnings.
This fall, the artist will be in residence at Soho Revue working on a collection exploring the Greek tale of Daphne, who morphed into a laurel tree, as a way to conceptualize transformation amid climate catastrophe. Keep up with that new series on Instagram.

title: Pattern and Bold, Saturated Color Commingle in Ben Sledsens' Rhythmic Paintings
description: In Ben Sledsens’ new body of work, An Apple for the Road, saturated fields of color meet methodical patterns constructed from grasses, leaves, bri
body:
In Ben Sledsens’ new body of work, An Apple for the Road, saturated fields of color meet methodical patterns constructed from grasses, leaves, brick, and more. The Antwerp-born artist conceives of vibrant, atmospheric paintings in which life pauses for a moment: there’s a swan hovering over its tinted reflection, a woman just stepping out her front door, and vivid still lifes in which clouds and soft breezes rustle through the windows.
Often beginning with drawings on paper before translating the most salient details to the canvas, Sledsens is interested in repetition and the visual power of pattern, which he layers to form dense thickets of willow trees or the tiles lining a boating dock. These motifs set the scene, in which the ordinary appears in a new, slightly skewed perspective.
“Lily in the Blue Pond” (2025), oil and acrylic on canvas, 180 x 150 centimeters
While bold in color, the oil-and-acrylic paintings are quiet and intimate. Sledsens beckons the viewer into domestic spaces and serene pockets of landscape, while opting for soft light and the haze of dusk. By pairing recognizable imagery with a sense that we’re witnessing a fleeting moment, the artist invites questions about what sustains our attentions and what details we may never fully grasp.
An Apple for the Road is on view from September 3 to October 10 at Tim Van Laere Galler in Antwerp. Dive into the artist’s archive on Instagram.

title: 'Handmade Utopia' Relishes the Architecture of California's Back-to-the-Land Movement
description: When I was about 10 years old, my parents organized a vacation to a tiny enclave called Orr Hot Springs just outside of Ukiah, California. Nestled
body:
When I was about 10 years old, my parents organized a vacation to a tiny enclave called Orr Hot Springs just outside of Ukiah, California. Nestled in the mountains with a history dating to 1858 as a stagecoach stop with redwoods shading the trails, the property has a uniquely layered architectural history. We stayed in what my dad called “Art’s cabin,” which turned out to have really been built by a guy named Art in the mid-1970s. A giant tree intersected the middle of the structure.
Art’s cabin is one of few remaining buildings from the property’s back-to-the-land era, before it became today’s modern yet earthy resort. In 1974, my dad and a group of friends from Berkeley teamed up to buy the hot springs. Over time, a small community developed as people purchased “shares” in the property. Attracted by the cooperative nature of the place and the opportunity to escape the city, people came and went, sometimes staying for a couple of weeks and sometimes for a couple of years. To make income, my dad recalls leading week-long carpentry courses, during which visitors and community members alike constructed what he describes as tiny, “very not-code” cabins, some of which were finished and actually lived in for a time. There was a buzz around building.

As my dad and I both paged through my hot-off-the-press copy of Handmade Utopia: Back-to-the-Land Architecture in Northern California, published by DAP/Edition Patrick Frey, I could tell that a lot jogged his memory. I grew up hearing stories about the ups and downs of running an intentional community in the hills during the 1970s, and his experience is but one among many thousands. Having also lived in Humboldt County for a time myself, I enjoy the striking sense of continuity throughout the past five decades that author David Jacob Kramer and photographer Michael Schmelling capture in this hefty tome. The work represents a counterculture that, though changed, is still alive and well.
The vernacular of Northern California architecture in the late 1960s and 1970s is a result of resourcefulness, timeliness, and a staunch desire to do things one’s own way. Scrounged from discarded redwood left over by the region’s logging industry and salvaged architectural details and appliances from historical homes, the houses cover a broad range of styles. Think triangular windows, diagonal paneling, cylindrical or octagonal footprints, and ad hoc additions.
Often, builders had no plan, constructing their dwellings to whatever standard they were able. They used plastic to cover windows and sometimes innovated with compositing toilet solutions or solar. The buildings were hardly ever up to code, and many lived with the constant anxiety that their homes could be condemned and they’d be evicted by local authorities. But the risk outweighed a mainstream alternative that felt too limiting or oppressive. “In pursuit of something better, back-to-the-landers radically reappraised what a home could and should be—and how it might inform the lives of its inhabitants,” Kramer says in the introductory essay.
Some homes of the era draw their inspiration from Buckminster Fuller’s geodesic dome design, while others take cues from neolithic forms or Indigenous structures around the world. Many examples of these were published contemporaneously in popular books like Lloyd Kahn’s Shelter, which itself was a spinoff of his editorial contributions to Stewart Brand’s counterculture magazine, Whole Earth Catalog. The legendary publication described itself as an “access device” that served as a kind of ultimate peer-to-peer DIY guide for living and building.

My first impression of Handmade Utopia was that it felt like a kind of reverent extension of Barry Shapiro and Art Boericke’s seminal 1973 photo book Handmade Houses: A Guide to the Woodbutcher’s Art. By comparison, this fresh look at the stylistic movement is a more personal expression of wonder and fondness for not only a particular style of architecture but the societal complexities that spawned it.
Kramer and Schmelling adventured through the NorCal countryside over the course of four years to touch base with people who still make their homes in the woods. Even those who no longer live in their decades-old dwellings can retrace their steps to see what remains. And the foundation of every one is composed of ingenuity and independent spirit. In addition to thoughtful introductory texts, the bulk of the book is chock full of photographs, archival material, and anecdotes by the folks whose structures the authors visit.
Rather than a comprehensive study of hand-built Northern California architecture, Handmade Utopia reads more like an homage to what Kramer calls the “audacious hope” of the back-to-the-land movement. And this hope isn’t relegated to its historical roots, as young people today are confronted by the prohibitive cost of both homes and land. “Schmelling and I felt an urgency in capturing these homes before they literally went back-to-the-land, disappearing along with the generation who built them,” Kramer says.
Handmade Utopia is officially slated for release on September 1. Find your copy in the Colossal Shop. You might also enjoy a tour of Ricky Boscarino’s whimiscal hand-built home in New Jersey or Matt Bua’s “repurposed city” in Upstate New York.

title: Mischievous Cats Rule in Minyoung Kim's Affectionately Quirky Paintings
description: Myriad myths and symbols are wrapped up in our captivation with cats. In ancient Egypt, the animals were revered as divine protectors, personified
body:
Myriad myths and symbols are wrapped up in our captivation with cats. In ancient Egypt, the animals were revered as divine protectors, personified by the deity Bastet. In Japan, it’s hard to walk by shops without seeing a maneki-neko waving from the window. And superstition says that if a black cat crosses your path, it may be bad luck. Although depending who you ask, it could mean good luck… did you happen to notice which direction it was walking?
For artist Minyoung Kim, who centers black felines in her eccentric compositions, the fascination comes down to “the contrast between how ordinary and how weird they are,” she tells Colossal. Kim taps into the paradoxes, such as how the animals can be seemingly everywhere in our daily lives, yet they often remain aloof and unreadable.
“Cat Sock” (2024), oil on canvas, 100 x 100 centimeters
That tinge of mischief is something she pulls through each work. “I want the painting to look visually inviting or polished at first glance, but as you stand there, you start noticing things that don’t quite add up—a reflection that’s wrong, an odd shape, an absurd gesture. That tiny moment of ‘Wait, what?’ is where the magic happens for me.”
The black creatures in particular stoke Kim’s imagination because they carry the most “heavy cultural baggage,” she says. “Over time, the black cat in my work became less of a subject and more of a tool: sometimes a good luck charm, sometimes just a way to inject a bit of humour or subtle weirdness into a scene.” Rarely a passive element of the compositions, the feisty pets often appear to be plotting something devious involving cutlery or simply creating chaos.
Nuanced, slightly strange elements are characteristic of the artist’s work, in which she toys with scale and absurd compositions. Sometimes the cats are more or less realistic, while other times their faces appear on tiny, fuzzy balls or critters, such as in “Cocktail Party” or “Chopped Melon.” Kim says, “Humour is huge for me. Even though my paintings are pretty tightly constructed and technically meticulous, I really don’t want them to feel stiff or overly academic. I want them to have a sense of play.”
Often, only a paw or a tail is visible, rendered mid-swipe as claws extend to grip a tablecloth or reach out to grab a knife. “Just dropping a random paw, a single eye, or a curved tail into an otherwise mundane setup completely shifts the mood,” Kim says. “It interrupts the room…Ultimately, it’s about making the familiar feel just a little off.”
“The Shining Net” (2026), oil on linen, 25.5 x 20.3 centimeters
Over time, Kim has thoughtfully transitioned how felines appear in her pieces. In her most recent paintings, such as “The Shining Net,” the pattern of a moth’s wings allude to the yellow eyes, but the artist instead emphasizes other symbolic and compositional forms, such as water droplets and an intricate web. Lately, she has been interested in European still-life painting, “specifically how it handles light, liquids, reflections, and moments of visual illusion,” she says.
Kim is currently preparing for a solo booth at Untitled Art, Miami Beach, where she’ll exhibit with Enari Gallery. Follow updates and see more on Instagram.
